title: The Virgin Birth and Isaiah 7:14

keyTerms.d: That Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin, without a human father, by the creative power of God’s Spirit. It is not a claim about Mary’s perpetual virginity, nor (in the New Testament texts themselves) about a painless or miraculous delivery, nor about the immaculate conception of Mary herself — distinct doctrines, held by some Christian traditions and not others, that should not be confused with the New Testament assertion itself.

Matthew 1–2 and Luke 1–2 are widely regarded by scholars as literarily independent: they share almost no wording, sequence their events differently, and cannot easily be derived one from the other. Matthew works largely through Joseph’s experience, Luke largely through Mary’s.

Across that independence the two accounts converge on a striking cluster of agreements — virginal conception, the name Jesus given by angelic command, birth at Bethlehem, descent from David, and the role of the Holy Spirit. Independent witnesses agreeing on a core is the kind of thing historians take seriously, even when they dispute the details.

A pregnancy before the couple “came together” carried, in first-century Judaism, the unavoidable shadow of illegitimacy. A church fabricating a flattering origin story would have had easier options than one that handed its opponents this weapon. The awkwardness is evidence not that the conception was virginal, but that something about Jesus’ origin was, from very early, in need of explanation.

The Hebrew word Isaiah uses is ‘almah, which means a young woman of marriageable age. It does not strictly mean “virgin”; Hebrew’s closer term is betulah. An ‘almah was typically presumed unmarried and so presumably a virgin, but the term’s focus is youth, not sexual status.

What Matthew quotes is not the Hebrew but the Septuagint — the pre-Christian Greek translation made by Jews, which rendered ‘almah with the Greek parthenos, “virgin.” Matthew did not engineer that rendering; he inherited it.

A prophecy that had a real meaning for Ahaz’s own day and a fuller resonance that Matthew, looking back through the resurrection, found realized in Christ. This is a contested, largely typological case, not a knockdown prediction: Isaiah 7:14 is best treated as a window, not a proof.

The pagan tales, where they involve miraculous birth at all, are overwhelmingly stories of divine impregnation: a god, in some bodily or quasi-bodily form, unites with a mortal woman, who then is no longer a virgin. A virginal conception is a woman conceiving with no consort, divine or human, by the non-sexual creative act of God’s Spirit.

derive.q: Two infancy accounts share almost no wording and sequence their events differently — yet both report the virginal conception, the angel-given name, Bethlehem, Davidic descent and the Spirit’s role — so the core is…?
derive.why: If Matthew and Luke had collaborated, their agreements would prove little. If they had simply copied a common source, we would expect verbal overlap. Instead we find two writers, working from different angles, who nonetheless land on the same astonishing core.

derive.q: Matthew shows Joseph “resolved to divorce her quietly,” and hostile traditions later charged an irregular union — so the awkwardness shows…?
derive.ans: that Jesus’ origin needed explaining — not, by itself, that the conception was virginal
derive.why: That is a detail no early Christian eager to defend Jesus’ honor would invent gratuitously; a church fabricating a flattering origin story would have had easier options. The awkwardness is itself a fragment of evidence — not that the conception was virginal, but that something about Jesus’ origin was, from very early, in need of explanation.

derive.q: Within roughly a generation of the Gospels, the virginal conception is listed among the “mysteries to be cried aloud” and simply assumed, not argued for — so it was…?
derive.ans: received tradition rather than fresh invention
derive.why: The doctrine is not a medieval accretion. Ignatius of Antioch, writing around AD 110, already lists “the virginity of Mary and her child-bearing” among the “mysteries to be cried aloud” — suggesting it was received tradition rather than fresh invention.

derive.q: Luke never quotes Isaiah 7:14, yet still reports a virginal conception — so the belief…?
derive.ans: does not derive from the verse
derive.why: The earliest tradition rests on the events Matthew and Luke report; Isaiah is cited to interpret, not to generate, the claim. Strip the verse away entirely and Luke still reports a virginal conception. On this reading the conviction came first, and the text was seen, in hindsight, to illumine it.

derive.q: In the pagan tales a god unites with a mortal woman, who then is no longer a virgin — so the alleged parallel is…?
derive.ans: a disanalogy — and the reply is a negative argument only
derive.why: None of these is a virginal conception — a woman conceiving with no consort, divine or human, by the non-sexual creative act of God’s Spirit. That said, this is a negative argument — it shows the borrowing thesis is weak, not that the conception occurred.

derive.q: A private, miraculous event attested by two sources a generation or two after the fact — can historical method alone settle it?
derive.why: No purely historical method can adjudicate a private, miraculous event attested by two sources a generation or two after the fact. That is the real limit of the evidence, and it should be stated without flinching. The early, independent, embarrassing profile of the tradition gives it real evidential weight; it does not amount to proof.

honestState.p1: Conservative scholars hold that the convergence and the embarrassment criterion make a virginal conception the best explanation of the data. Critical scholars such as Brown judge that historical method alone cannot settle the question; others, more skeptical, judge it a relatively late confessional development. No purely historical method can adjudicate a private, miraculous event attested by two sources a generation or two after the fact. That is the real limit of the evidence, and it should be stated without flinching.
honestState.fairness: Among Jewish interpreters, the reading of Isaiah 7:14 as a near-term sign to Ahaz, with ‘almah meaning simply “young woman,” is the mainstream and longstanding view, and Christians should state that reading accurately rather than caricature it. The silence of Paul, Mark and John is a real datum, not a trick. And the proposed harmonizations of the two genealogies are reconstructions, not statements the texts themselves make; a fair reader should label them contested.
honestState.verdict: The virgin birth is not a public, multiply-corroborated event like the crucifixion under Pilate. It is the testimony of two Gospels, early and independent, agreeing on a core that ran against the church’s social interest. Those features give it real evidential weight; they do not amount to proof. The case clears the mistranslation and borrowing charges, and it cannot, by historical method alone, prove a private miracle. But an early, independently attested tradition that embarrassed its own tellers fits the confession better than its rivals — and for anyone persuaded on other grounds that God raised Jesus from the dead, a miraculous beginning is no great leap. So our answer is yes: Jesus, truly God and truly man, was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and what exactly is being claimed.
cards.a: Matthew and Luke attest the virgin conception through visibly independent accounts, agreeing on the core. The claim is the virginal conception — that Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin, without a human father, by the creative power of God’s Spirit — a creedal affirmation resting on the testimony of two Gospels, held by faith with reasons, not demonstrated like a theorem.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: The claim carried a heavy embarrassment cost: a pregnancy before the couple “came together” carried the unavoidable shadow of illegitimacy, and a fabricating church had easier options. Limit: the awkwardness is evidence not that the conception was virginal, but that something about Jesus’ origin was, from very early, in need of explanation.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That an early, independently attested tradition that embarrassed its own tellers fits the confession better than its rivals: real weight, not proof. It is not a public event open to investigation the way the crucifixion is, and it cannot, by historical method alone, prove a private miracle.

cards.q: Why does the agreement of the two infancy accounts carry weight?
cards.a: Because of how it is structured. Had they collaborated, their agreements would prove little; had they copied a common source, we would expect verbal overlap. Instead two writers, working from different angles, land on the same core — which pushes the tradition back behind both Gospels into an earlier, shared stream, though that stream need not reach all the way back to the event itself.

cards.q: How early is the doctrine, and what does its treatment suggest?
cards.a: It is not a medieval accretion. Within roughly a generation of the Gospels, the virginal conception is simply assumed, not argued for — suggesting it was received tradition rather than fresh invention.

cards.q: What does ‘almah mean — and what should be conceded?
cards.a: A young woman of marriageable age. It does not strictly mean “virgin”; Hebrew’s closer term is betulah, and the term’s focus is youth, not sexual status. Isaiah 7:14 is a contested, largely typological case, not a knockdown prediction — and the virgin birth does not stand or fall on the translation of ‘almah.

cards.q: Where did the reading “virgin” in Matthew’s quotation come from?
cards.a: From the Septuagint — the pre-Christian Greek translation made by Jews, which rendered ‘almah with parthenos, “virgin.” Matthew did not engineer that rendering; he inherited it.

cards.q: How is Isaiah 7:14 best read — and what role does it play in the case?
cards.a: On the reading the essay takes, as dual fulfilment: a word with a real meaning for Ahaz’s own day and a fuller resonance that Matthew, looking back, found realized in Christ. The conviction came first and the text was seen, in hindsight, to illumine it. It is a window, not a proof — as a standalone argument it does not work, and the case should not be hung on it.

cards.q: Reply to: Matthew built a doctrine on a mistranslation.
cards.a: Concede the factual kernel, not the inference: ‘almah is not betulah, and the verse is not a slam-dunk prediction. But the virgin birth does not derive from Isaiah 7:14 — Isaiah is cited to interpret, not to generate, the claim. Strip the verse away and Luke, who never quotes it, still reports a virginal conception. The objection wounds a bad argument, not the doctrine.

cards.q: Reply to: it is borrowed pagan mythology — and what is the reply’s limit?
cards.a: The pagan tales are stories of divine impregnation — a god unites with a mortal woman, who then is no longer a virgin; none is a virginal conception by the non-sexual creative act of God’s Spirit. And a fiercely monotheistic Jewish community would hardly import a god siring children on women. Limit: this is a negative argument — it shows the borrowing thesis is weak, not that the conception occurred.

cards.q: Reply to: Paul, Mark and John are silent, so it was invented later.
cards.a: The silence is a real datum, not a trick — but silence is not denial. Paul wrote occasional letters, not biographies; Mark begins at the Jordan by literary design. Nor is the silence total: Mark alone calls Jesus “the son of Mary,” and John’s opponents retort, “We were not born of sexual immorality” — hints, not proofs. And two independent witnesses push the tradition earlier, not later.

cards.q: Reply to: the genealogies and itineraries contradict each other.
cards.a: The tensions are real, and the proposed harmonizations are reconstructions a fair reader should label contested. But the tensions do not touch the shared core: two accounts that disagree on route and lineage yet agree on virginal conception, Bethlehem, and Davidic descent look less like one fabricated story than like two independent memories of the same extraordinary claim.

obj.q: Isaiah’s Hebrew says ‘almah — a young woman, not a virgin. Matthew built a doctrine on a Greek mistranslation; the whole edifice is a linguistic accident.
obj.model: I concede its factual kernel, not its inference. Isaiah’s ‘almah is not betulah, and the verse is not a slam-dunk prediction — in its setting it was a sign to King Ahaz. But the “virgin” reading was no Christian invention: the pre-Christian Greek translation made by Jews rendered ‘almah with parthenos, and Matthew inherited it. More importantly, the virgin birth does not derive from Isaiah 7:14. The earliest tradition rests on the events Matthew and Luke report; Isaiah is cited to interpret, not to generate, the claim. Strip the verse away entirely and Luke — who never quotes it — still reports a virginal conception. So the objection wounds a bad argument, not the doctrine itself.

obj.q: Paul, our earliest writer, never mentions it — he says only that Jesus was “born of woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4) and “descended from David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). Mark, the earliest Gospel, has no infancy narrative at all; John never mentions Mary’s virginity. Only two New Testament voices attest it — it grew up as legend in the decades between Paul and Matthew and Luke.
obj.model: The honest concession: attestation is limited to two Gospels, and silence in Paul and Mark is a real datum, not a trick. But silence is not denial — Paul’s “born of woman” and “descended from David according to the flesh” are phrases that neither affirm nor require a virginal conception, and Paul wrote occasional letters to churches, not biographies, and had no obvious occasion to discuss Jesus’ conception; Mark begins his story at the Jordan as a matter of literary design. Nor is the silence total: Mark alone calls Jesus “the son of Mary” rather than the son of Joseph, and in John his opponents retort, “We were not born of sexual immorality” — hints, not proofs. And because the two writers who did tell the birth story did so independently, their agreement pushes the tradition back behind both Gospels into an earlier, shared stream — though that stream need not reach all the way back to the event itself. What the argument from silence cannot do is convert an early, independently attested conviction into a late invention.

obj.q: Virgin births are standard mythology — Mithras, Dionysus, the divine paternity of Augustus. Christians gave their hero the usual upgrade.
obj.model: This must be taken seriously, not waved away — but the reply turns on a disanalogy that holds up well. The pagan tales, where they involve miraculous birth at all, are overwhelmingly stories of divine impregnation: Dionysus is the offspring of Zeus and the mortal Semele; the Augustus legend has Apollo as a physical agent; Mithras is born from a rock, with no woman in the scene at all. None of these is a virginal conception — a woman conceiving with no consort, divine or human, by the non-sexual creative act of God’s Spirit. And the last thing a fiercely monotheistic Palestinian Jewish community would import is a god siring children on women. The candid verdict, even among many non-confessional historians, is that the parallels are too loose and too late to ground a derivation. That said, this is a negative argument — it shows the borrowing thesis is weak, not that the conception occurred.

obj.q: Matthew and Luke can’t even agree on Jesus’ grandfather or on whether the family went to Egypt. Why trust either on the conception?
obj.model: Grant the tensions: Matthew traces Joseph’s line through Solomon to a father named Jacob, Luke through Nathan to a father named Heli; Matthew has a flight to Egypt, Luke a return to Nazareth. Proposed harmonizations exist — that Luke records Mary’s line, or that levirate marriage explains the two fathers — but they are reconstructions, not statements the texts themselves make, and should be labelled contested. What the tensions do not touch is the shared core. Two accounts that disagree on route and lineage yet agree on virginal conception, Bethlehem, and Davidic descent look less like one fabricated story than like two independent memories of the same extraordinary claim, each elaborated in its own way.

unseen.q: You call the illegitimacy charge embarrassing — but maybe the rumor was simply true. Read closely, the infancy narratives themselves quietly preserve an illegitimate conception, and the virgin birth is the pious cover story.
unseen.model: That is the skeptic’s standard reply to the embarrassment argument — a view revived, in a variant of her own, by Jane Schaberg. But the explicit charge of an irregular union surfaces in our sources only after Matthew, and it reads most naturally as a hostile answer to the Christian claim rather than independent memory; a community inventing a cover would hardly have told a story that kept the scandal in view. Schaberg’s variant also runs against the texts’ plain sense: Matthew places the conception “from the Holy Spirit” before Joseph and Mary “came together” (Matthew 1:18–20), and Luke’s Mary asks how she can conceive “since I am a virgin” (Luke 1:34–35). The embarrassment still shows only that Jesus’ origin needed explaining from very early; the case for the virginal conception rests on the two independent accounts.
